structure.title: ESG factors in business strategy, governance and risk management
structure.heading: 1 ESG factors in business strategy, governance and risk management
structure.start_phrase: This chapter provides an overview of Nordea’s ESG -related business strategy, governance and risk management.
structure.summary:
- Purpose and scope: Overview of how Nordea integrates ESG factors into business strategy, governance, and risk management, with detailed E, S and G sections to follow.
- Definition and risk transmission: ESG factors can affect financial, environmental, social, or governance performance/solvency and act as risk drivers across traditional prudential risks (credit, market, business model, operational—including reputational/legal—and liquidity) and their sub-categories; these are cross-mapped to Nordea’s Common Risk Taxonomy.
- Double materiality approach: In line with CSRD, Nordea maps both its impacts on people and planet and the impacts of ESG factors on the bank and its counterparties.
- Materiality assessment (MA): A climate and nature-related MA, leveraging ICLAAP and a 4-level risk materiality banding, embeds climate and environmental (C&E) risk drivers.
- Key findings and capital impact: The 2024 MA indicates material exposure to multiple C&E risk drivers, mainly via counterparties; Nordea reserved additional capital in 2024 for climate-related credit risk; a CSRD-aligned Double Materiality Assessment (DMA) was also performed.
- Risk strategy and transition: Nordea’s strategy is to actively engage customers to drive sustainability transitions, mitigate identified C&E risks, and capture growth opportunities.
- Strategic pillars: Sustainability efforts center on four areas—financial strength, climate and environmental action, social responsibility, and governance and culture—linked to relevant UN SDGs and material topics.
- Business model resilience: Dependent on counterparties’ sustainability and effective risk mitigation; aims to align on-balance sheet lending and investments with the Paris Agreement via reductions in financed GHG emissions.
- Products, funding, and liquidity: ESG-related offerings support customer transition and integrate sustainability into funding and liquidity strategies, including sustainability-linked funding activities.
- Targets and implementation: Internal targets to cut operational GHG emissions by 40–50% by 2030 and reach net zero by 2050; interim portfolio targets guide net-zero steering; integration into lending/investment policies and practices.
- External frameworks and commitments: Engagement with Principles for Responsible Banking, UN Global Compact, Equator Principles, Poseidon Principles, and other industry standards.

nodes.title: ESG FACTORS IN BUSINESS STRATEGY: INTRODUCTION
nodes.heading: 1.1 ESG FACTORS IN BUSINESS STRATEGY: INTRODUCTION
nodes.start_phrase: Environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors are the characteristics potentially positively or negatively impacting the ﬁnancial, environmental, social or governance performance or solvency of Nordea or its counterparties, across value chains or business environments.
nodes.summary:
- Purpose and scope: Overview of Nordea’s ESG-related business strategy, governance and risk management, with detailed E, S and G sections to follow.
- ESG as risk drivers: ESG factors can positively or negatively affect Nordea or its counterparties and transmit primarily through traditional prudential risk categories (credit, market, business model, operational including reputational and legal, liquidity, and sub-categories), and via actions Nordea takes on material sustainability impacts. ESG ambition and risk management are cross-mapped to Nordea’s Common Risk Taxonomy.
- Double materiality foundation: Strategy and risk alignment are based on systematic identification and mapping of ESG factors via transmission channels to operations, business model and risk profile, using the CSRD’s double materiality concept (impacts on planet/society and on Nordea/counterparties).
- 2024 materiality assessment (MA): A climate and nature-related MA, leveraging ICLAAP and a 4-level risk materiality banding, identifies material exposure to climate and environmental risk drivers across prudential risks, mainly via counterparties. Additional capital was reserved in 2024 for climate-related credit risk. Results also informed a CSRD-aligned double materiality assessment (DMA).
- Risk strategy and positioning: Nordea aims to actively support a sustainability-based transition through customer engagement while capturing growth opportunities, with risk mitigants for identified C&E drivers. Sustainability efforts center on four areas: financial strength; climate and environmental action; social responsibility; and governance and culture, linked to relevant UN SDGs and areas of material impact through lending, investments and operations.
- Paris alignment and products: Objective to align on-balance sheet lending and investments with the Paris Agreement by reducing financed GHG emissions. ESG-related products, customer and investee engagement, and sustainability-linked funding integrate sustainability into funding and liquidity strategies.
- Targets and policies: Internal targets to reduce GHG emissions 40–50% by 2030 and achieve net zero by 2050. Interim portfolio targets support net zero steering and balance sheet alignment with policy and best practice. Commitments embedded in lending/investment policies and internal frameworks (procurement, travel, conduct) and anchored in initiatives such as PRB, UN Global Compact, Equator Principles and Poseidon Principles. Mitigations include industry credit policies, corporate transition plans, customer ESG assessments and monitoring of energy performance certificates.
- Biodiversity integration: 2024 position on biodiversity and nature-related impacts adopted for incorporation into strategy, governance and risk management toward 2025. Biodiversity included in business environment scanning; sector guidelines updated (with general and sector-specific expectations in agriculture, aquaculture, feed and food processing, and real estate). Capacity building, training and initial dependency/impact assessments using the WWF Biodiversity Risk Filter and ENCORE conducted. 2025 plans include enhanced, quantified biodiversity assessments across the value chain focused on the lending portfolio.
- Reporting and regulation: CSRD applies from 2024, replacing NFRD; Nordea reports under ESRS in the 2024 Annual Report and benchmarked against draft EBA ESG risk management guidelines to prepare for finalization.
- EU Taxonomy and KPIs: Disclosure of taxonomy-eligible and taxonomy-aligned exposures under Article 8, with Green Asset Ratio (GAR) KPIs showing the share of taxonomy-aligned assets. 2024 scope includes retail exposures (per internal methodology), NFRD undertakings (financial and non-financial), local government financing, collateral obtained (real estate) and off-balance sheet exposures, with details in the Annual Report and GAR templates.
- Visual framework: Reference to a figure outlining how ESG-related objectives, targets and limits are aligned within business and risk strategies.

nodes.title: Reporting and EU Taxonomy
nodes.heading: 1.1.1 Reporting and EU Taxonomy
nodes.start_phrase: As of 2024, the CSRD applies to Nordea.
nodes.summary:
- Embedding sustainability commitments into Nordea’s internal policy frameworks (procurement, travel, employee conduct) and aligning with climate benchmarks and GHG reduction targets.
- Implementing mitigation measures beyond GHG targets, including industry credit policies, corporate transition plans, customer ESG assessments, and monitoring of energy performance certificates.
- Advancing biodiversity integration: a 2024-approved biodiversity position to be embedded in strategy, governance and risk management toward 2025; inclusion of biodiversity in the 2024 Business Environment Scanning; updated sector guidelines (general plus agriculture, aquaculture, feed and food processing, and real estate), with further enhancements planned in 2025.
- Building capabilities through methodologies, data foundations, trainings and internal dialogues; initial value-chain dependency and impact assessments using WWF Biodiversity Risk Filter and ENCORE; 2025 plan to quantify dependencies/impacts, focus on the lending portfolio, and drive targeted actions to reduce downstream risks and capture opportunities.
- Reporting transition to CSRD from 2024, applying ESRS and the double materiality concept; feasibility and benchmarking work to prepare for the EBA guidelines on ESG risk.
- EU Taxonomy compliance under Article 8: disclosure of taxonomy-eligible and -aligned exposures; reporting Green Asset Ratio KPIs and details in the 2024 Annual Report and GAR templates 6, 7, and 8.
- Scope for 2024 disclosures includes retail exposures, exposures to undertakings under NFRD (financial and non-financial), local government financing, collateral obtained by possession (residential and commercial properties), and off-balance sheet exposures.
- Reference to an overarching approach (Figure 1) for aligning ESG objectives, targets and limits across business and risk strategies.

nodes.title: ESG FACTORS GOVERNANCE: INTRODUCTION
nodes.heading: 1.2 ESG FACTORS GOVERNANCE: INTRODUCTION
nodes.start_phrase: Nordea has embedded oversight of strategic steering for material ESG impacts within its Group governance model (Figure X).
nodes.summary:
- Overview of Nordea’s ESG governance framework and how ESG oversight is embedded in Group governance.
- Board roles and committees:
  - Board sets purpose, values, and strategic direction for sustainability; ensures compatibility with a sustainable economy transition.
  - BOSC advises and recommends strategic sustainability priorities for Board approval.
  - BRIC oversees financial impacts of ESG, Group risk profile, and key ESG risk developments.
  - BAC oversees sustainability reporting, including regulatory disclosures and related controls.
- Group Leadership Team and executive committees:
  - Group CEO proposes strategic sustainability priorities and sets related targets.
  - SEC oversees business implementation of sustainability and facilitates operational ESG risk management.
  - RC oversees ESG-related risk strategy and policy framework; sub-committees address ESG topics within their mandates.
  - ALCO sets principles for performance management and financial planning frameworks.
  - ESG Reporting Sub-committee supports sustainability disclosures and methodologies, particularly financed emissions used in the risk appetite framework.
- Board effectiveness and capability:
  - Annual suitability assessments of individual Board members and the Board as a whole inform training.
  - 2024 trainings covered facilitated/financed emissions, customer engagement, social responsibility/just transition, Nordic energy transition, and emission removals/offsetting.
- Credit risk governance:
  - ESG-related risks in credit processes follow delegated decision-making; high ESG-risk customers are escalated to higher-level credit committees.
- Group-wide implementation:
  - ESG programme (established 2021) ensures consistent ESG integration across 1st and 2nd lines of defence and addresses regulatory change.
  - Overseen by an Operational Steering Committee co-chaired by the Chief of Staff and Head of Group Credit Risk Control; involves all business areas, Group functions, risk areas, Group Financial Management, and Risk Control.
  - 2024 focus on building the ESG Data Foundation to enable data-driven portfolio steering, enhance ESG risk management, disclosures, and management oversight.

nodes.title: ESG factors in group governance
nodes.heading: 1.2.1 ESG factors in group governance

nodes.title: ESG factors in organisational structure and reporting
nodes.heading: 1.2.3 ESG factors in organisational structure and reporting
nodes.start_phrase: ESG is an integrated component of existing processes for decision -making, risk management, escalation and reporting across the three LoDs .
nodes.summary:
- ESG is embedded into decision-making, risk management, escalation, and reporting via a three lines of defense (LoD) model.
- Responsibilities by LoD:
  - 1st LoD: Sets and implements strategic responses and mitigations for ESG impacts/risks; Chief of Staff ensures coordination.
  - 2nd LoD: Develops the Sustainability and ESG policy framework and oversees 1st LoD implementation; Head of GCRC coordinates as policy owner.
  - 3rd LoD: Provides independent assurance and advice on ESG-related risks.
- Coordination and roles:
  - Each LoD appoints an ESG coordinator/ambassador.
  - Group Sustainability coordinates 1st LoD; GCRC coordinates 2nd LoD; Group Internal Audit plans ESG assurance coverage based on risk assessment.
  - Cross-risk coordination mandated for key topics (e.g., greenwashing) and for ESG reporting aggregation to ensure consistent framework implementation.
- Competence and training:
  - Three-layer training approach: (1) general mandatory Code of Conduct e-learning plus optional ESG e-learnings and regulatory updates; (2) tailored training for roles directly working with ESG; (3) in-depth training for selected groups.
  - Group Risk prioritizes nature risk analysis and financed emissions accounting; Group Compliance completes targeted trainings on ESG regulatory requirements, terminology, and EU Taxonomy.
- Board-level ESG reporting (aggregated and quarterly):
  - Sustainability Roadmap monitoring of strategic progress and targets, including voluntary and supervisory commitments.
  - ESG Management Report: exposures by group/business area/sector/product; historical and forecast financed emissions; EU Taxonomy eligible/aligned assets; sustainable finance/funding/savings volumes; ESG data quality indicators and progress tracking.
  - Group Risk Report: risk appetite monitoring for ESG cross-risk concentrations and financed emissions per the Common Risk Taxonomy.
  - Other risk reports: financed emissions by business area, geography, industry, and customer; climate physical and nature-related risk concentration; mitigation status and coverage.
  - Embedded ESG within ICAAP (capital adequacy, stress testing, scenarios); 2nd LoD reporting on ESG embedment (e.g., Group Compliance Report).
- Remuneration alignment with ESG:
  - ESG goals integrated across variable pay plans and the long-term incentive plan; Group Pool funding and profit sharing link pay to green financing (per the Green Financing Framework) and Sustainability Roadmap goals.
  - ESG scorecards support ambitions to 2025.
  - Senior leaders’ incentives tied to progress on the Sustainability Roadmap, increased green financing volumes, and improved gender balance in senior leadership, alongside non-financial KPIs (employee engagement, customer satisfaction, risk/compliance/conduct).
  - A material portion of GLT and senior leaders’ non-financial remuneration is linked to ESG factors.

nodes.title: Remuneration
nodes.heading: 1.2.4 Remuneration
nodes.start_phrase: Nordea has integrated ESG goals in all Group’s variable pay plans, extending it from the GLT and other senior leaders across the Nordea Group to variable pay participants through introduction of ESG -related goals to the Group Pool funding mechanism and more broadly to all employees by adding green ﬁnancing, deﬁned in accordance with Nordea’s Green Financing Framework, and Sustainability Roadmap goals in the proﬁt sharing plan.
nodes.summary:
- ESG governance is embedded across decision-making, risk management, escalation, and reporting through three Lines of Defense (LoDs).
- 1st LoD: accountable for strategic ESG response and risk mitigation; coordinated by the Chief of Staff.
- 2nd LoD: develops the Sustainability and ESG policy framework and oversees 1st LoD implementation; coordinated by the Head of GCRC as framework owner.
- 3rd LoD: provides independent assurance and advice on ESG-related risks.
- ESG coordinators/ambassadors are appointed within each LoD; Group Sustainability coordinates the 1st LoD, GCRC the 2nd LoD, and Group Internal Audit coordinates ESG assurance based on risk assessment.
- Cross-risk coordination is mandated for key topics (e.g., greenwashing) and processes (e.g., aggregation of ESG reporting) to ensure consistent implementation of the Sustainability and ESG Policy Framework.
- Competence building follows a three-layer training model: general mandatory ESG-integrated Code of Conduct and e-learnings; tailored training for roles working directly with ESG; and in-depth training for selected groups.
- Group Risk focuses on nature risk analysis and enhancing financed emissions accounting; Group Compliance completed mandatory ESG regulatory training, including EU Taxonomy.
- Quarterly ESG-specific Board reporting includes:
  - Sustainability Roadmap monitoring of strategic ESG implementation, targets, and commitments.
  - ESG Management Report on Group exposures, sector/product views, financed emissions (historical and forecast), EU Taxonomy eligibility/alignment, sustainable finance/funding/savings volumes, and ESG data quality indicators.
  - Group Risk Report covering ESG risk appetite, cross-risk concentrations, and financed emissions across the risk taxonomy.
  - Additional risk reports on financed emissions by business area/geography/industry/customer, climate physical risk, nature-related risk concentrations, and mitigation status.
  - ESG embedded in non-ESG reports (e.g., ICAAP stress testing and scenario analysis) and 2nd LoD reporting on ESG embedment (e.g., Group Compliance Report).
- Remuneration integrates ESG goals across variable pay, Group Pool funding, and profit sharing (aligned with Nordea’s Green Financing Framework and Sustainability Roadmap); ESG scorecards are included in long-term incentives.
- Senior leaders’ ESG remuneration goals target Sustainability Roadmap progress, increased green financing volumes, and improved gender balance in senior leadership, alongside non-financial KPIs (employee engagement, customer satisfaction, risk/compliance/conduct) and financial targets—making ESG a material component of leadership pay.

nodes.title: ESG FACTORS RISK MANAGEMENT: INTRODUCTION
nodes.heading: 1.3 ESG FACTORS RISK MANAGEMENT: INTRODUCTION
nodes.start_phrase: As part of the overall policy framework, the Sustainability and ESG Policy Framework speciﬁcally addresses the integration of ESG related items into the risk management cycle.
nodes.summary:
- Introduces Nordea’s Sustainability and ESG Policy Framework for integrating ESG considerations into the risk management cycle, grounded in Group Board Directives on Sustainability and Risk and aligned with CSRD double materiality.
- Defines ESG factors as environmental, social, or governance characteristics that can affect Nordea’s or its counterparties’ financial performance or solvency across value chains and time horizons.
- Details 2024 enhancements: updates to ESG risk identification and materiality assessment (MA), cascading into risk area documents and strategy-setting guidance; outlines 2025 focus on expanding identification/management of material ESG risks and strengthening monitoring and controls.
- Clarifies governance: GBD on Sustainability embeds impact materiality in business strategy; GBD on Risk embeds financial materiality in risk management; CEO Instruction (CEOI) on ESG Factors is the entry point for ESG materiality assessments.
- Notes 2024 approvals of the CRO Protocol on ESG-related risk and the Group Accountable Executive Protocol on Sustainability Strategy, which operationalize ESG integration into risk management and strategy, cascading to 1st and 2nd lines of defence.
- Presents the ESG Factor Taxonomy (initiated in 2021 and updated annually), aligned with EU Taxonomy, GRI 300, SASB, EBA guidance, ECB guide on climate and environmental risks, CSRD and ESRS, and other sources.
- Describes the materiality assessment approach: a Group-wide taxonomy of ESG risk drivers (hazards) and transmission channels derived from literature and validated with business and risk areas to reflect Nordea’s business model.
- Summarizes 2024 climate and nature-related MA: identification and assessment of C&E risk drivers across geographies, sectors, and portfolios over short, medium, long, and very long-term horizons; acknowledges potential impact on all prudential risks individually and in cross-risk views.
- States that the broader Double Materiality Assessment (DMA) in 2024 also evaluated social and governance aspects.
- Explains transmission channels as causal chains through which ESG drivers affect Nordea directly (own operations) or indirectly (via counterparties, invested assets, third parties), distinguishing economic transmissions (micro and macro real-economy effects) from financial transmissions (e.g., increased PDs in credit risk).
- Outlines management pathways: direct effects handled via internal governance and controls; indirect effects addressed through business and risk strategies and activity-level risk management.
- Notes a gross risk approach is used for identification (pre-mitigation) and defines impact durations: short (<1 year), medium (1–5), long (5–10), very long (10+ years).

nodes.title: Policy framework
nodes.heading: 1.3.1 Policy framework
nodes.start_phrase: As part of the overall policy framework, the Sustainability and ESG Policy Framework speciﬁcally addresses the integration of ESG related items into the risk management cycle.
nodes.summary:
- Establishes Nordea’s Sustainability and ESG Policy Framework for integrating ESG factors into the risk management cycle, grounded in Group Board Directives on Sustainability and Risk, and aligned with CSRD double materiality.
- Defines ESG factors as environmental, social, or governance characteristics affecting Nordea’s or counterparties’ financial performance or solvency across value chains and time horizons.
- Details 2024 enhancements: updated ESG risk identification and materiality assessment (MA), broader cascade into risk area documents and strategy-setting guidance; 2025 focus on extending material ESG risk management and strengthening monitoring and controls.
- Clarifies governance: GBD on Sustainability embeds impact materiality in strategy and governance; GBD on Risk embeds financial materiality in risk management and governance.
- Positions the CEO Instruction on ESG Factors as the starting point for ESG-related materiality assessments across the Group.
- Notes 2024 approvals of the CRO Protocol on ESG-related risk and the Group Accountable Executive Protocol on Sustainability Strategy, expanding financial and impact materiality in the Double Materiality Assessment (DMA) and cascading into 1st and 2nd lines of defense.
- Maintains an annually updated ESG Factor Taxonomy (since 2021) aligned with EU Taxonomy, GRI, SASB, EBA guidance, ECB climate and environmental risk guide, CSRD and ESRS, and other sources.
- Describes the materiality assessment approach: a Group-wide taxonomy of ESG risk drivers (hazards) and transmission channels, defined via literature and validated with business/risk areas for Nordea’s business model.
- Reports 2024 climate and nature-related MA identifying C&E risk drivers across geographies, sectors, and portfolios over short, medium, long, and very long-term horizons, with potential impacts across all prudential risks and cross-risk views; DMA also covers social and governance aspects.
- Explains transmission channels as causal chains affecting Nordea via its counterparties, invested assets, third parties, or own operations; distinguishes economic (micro/macro) from financial transmissions and maps them to prudential risk categories.
- Classifies effects as direct (managed via internal governance and controls) or indirect (managed via business/risk strategies) and applies a gross risk perspective (pre-mitigation), with defined impact durations: short (<1 year), medium (1–5 years), long (5–10 years), and very long (≥10 years).

nodes.title: Approach to the assessment of materiality of ESG factors
nodes.heading: 1.3.2 Approach to the assessment of materiality of ESG factors
nodes.start_phrase: Nordea has in place a Group -wide ESG Factor Taxonomy of ESG risk drivers (i.e. hazards) and a list of transmission channels.
nodes.summary:
- Overview and purpose: Introduces Nordea’s ESG Factors Risk Management approach and its integration into the overall risk management cycle through a Sustainability and ESG Policy Framework anchored in Group Board Directives (GBD) on Sustainability and on Risk, reflecting double materiality under CSRD.

- Definitions and governance: Defines ESG factors as environmental, social, or governance characteristics that can affect Nordea or its counterparties across time horizons and value chains. Clarifies governance split: GBD on Sustainability for impact materiality in business strategy; GBD on Risk for financial materiality in risk management. The CEO Instruction (CEOI) on ESG Factors is the entry point for Group-wide ESG materiality assessments.

- 2024–2025 developments: In 2024, updates enhanced ESG risk identification and materiality assessment (MA), with cascading into risk area documents and strategy-setting guidance. New protocols approved: CRO Protocol on ESG-related risks and Group Accountable Executive Protocol on Sustainability Strategy, detailing integration into risk and strategy frameworks and expanding double materiality assessment (DMA). 2025 focus will extend material ESG risk identification/management and strengthen monitoring and controls.

- ESG Factor Taxonomy: A Group-wide taxonomy of ESG risk drivers and transmission channels, first developed in 2021 and updated annually, aligned with EU Taxonomy, GRI, SASB, EBA guidance, ECB C&E risk guide, CSRD/ESRS, and other sources.

- Materiality assessment approach: Transmission channels are derived from literature and validated with business/risk areas to reflect Nordea’s business model. The 2024 enhanced climate and nature-related MA identified relevant C&E risk drivers across geographies, sectors, and portfolios over multiple time horizons (short <1y; medium 1–5y; long 5–10y; very long >10y). These drivers potentially affect all prudential risks individually and on a cross-risk basis. In parallel, the DMA added social and governance aspects.

- Transmission channels: Distinguishes economic transmissions (micro effects like operational disruptions from severe weather; macro effects like productivity shifts due to mitigation investments) that map to the broader economy, and financial transmissions that flow into Nordea’s risk profile (e.g., higher PDs in credit risk due to transition impacts). Classifies relationships into direct effects on Nordea (managed via internal governance/controls) and indirect effects via third parties/counterparties (managed via business and risk strategies). Risk identification uses a gross risk approach (pre-mitigation).

- Supporting tools: Heatmaps highlight industries and, for physical climate risks, countries/regions vulnerable to environmental factors. Used as a starting point in credit, market, and operational risk for portfolio classification and materiality assessment.

- Embedding in ICAAP/ILAAP and risk taxonomy: ESG factor materiality is assessed across all prudential risks within ICAAP/ILAAP. Where material, ESG-related risks must be embedded in the Common Risk Taxonomy and frameworks. ESG-related risks are Level 2 under credit risk; for other Level 1 risks (market, liquidity, capital/business model, operational, compliance), ESG-specific Level 3 risks are defined, including fair value market risk, financial reporting, reputational, outsourcing and third party, physical security, legal, technology, conduct and customer outcomes, governance, and people risks.

- Materiality criteria and bands: Materiality is assessed on a gross basis relative to total exposure. A four-band system determines materiality and impact:
  • Band 1: quantitative loss vs CET1; always material.
  • Band 2: quantitative loss vs CET1; requires qualitative expert judgment to determine materiality.
  • Band 3: qualitative criteria; always material.
  • Band 4: not meeting Bands 1–3; always non-material.
  Bands 2–3 rely on documented expert judgment. The assessment is reviewed annually via MA and ICLAAP.

- ESG Risk Appetite Framework (RAF): A dedicated ESG RAF defines risk statements, metrics, limits, and governance with monitoring/reporting at Group, branch, and subsidiary level. It ensures the ESG risk profile:
  • aligns with strategic sustainability objectives;
  • remains within financed emissions targets;
  • aligns with the business environment to avoid disruptive changes;
  • limits material cross-risk ESG concentrations;
  • stays within lower-level limits/controls of underlying prudential risks.

- Risk Appetite Statement (RAS): Since 2019, a Board-approved qualitative ESG RAS sets operating boundaries, requiring prudent management of material ESG exposures across all prudential risks, customer engagement to align with the Paris Agreement, and reduction of financed emissions over time.

- Metrics and limits: ESG RAF metrics exist at Levels 1–3 to control and monitor ESG-specific risks. Metric design considers:
  • consolidation/aggregation across risk areas and alignment with long/very long-term strategy and targets;
  • position within the Common Risk Taxonomy and focus on material, higher-impact ESG exposures;
  • strategic ambition, including Group commitments (e.g., financed emissions) and exclusions;
  • coherence with related metrics (e.g., tolerances for emissions restatements vs portfolio emissions trajectory).

nodes.title: ESG factors in Risk Appetite Framework
nodes.heading: 1.3.3 ESG factors in Risk Appetite Framework
nodes.start_phrase: As part of its prudent risk management, Nordea needs to ensure that risks driven by ESG factors (i.e. ESG Factor Taxonomy) are adequately managed and mitigated.
nodes.summary:
- Nordea uses ESG heatmaps to flag industries and regions potentially vulnerable to environmental and climate physical risks. These heatmaps are a starting point for deeper analysis and support credit, market, and operational risk identification, portfolio classification, and materiality assessment.

- ESG risk materiality is assessed within ICAAP and ILAAP across all prudential risks, informed by MA and DMA outputs. Where material, ESG risks are embedded in Nordea’s Common Risk Taxonomy and frameworks.

- Taxonomy placement: ESG-related risks are Level 2 under credit risk; for other Level 1 prudential risks (market, liquidity, capital/business model, operational, compliance), specific ESG Level 3 risks are defined, including fair value market risk, financial reporting, reputational, outsourcing/third party, physical security, legal, technology, conduct and customer outcomes, governance, and people risks.

- Materiality is assessed on a gross basis (ignoring mitigants) using a four-band scheme:
  - Band 1: quantitatively defined vs CET1; always material.
  - Band 2: quantitatively defined vs CET1; requires expert judgment to confirm materiality.
  - Band 3: qualitatively defined; always material.
  - Band 4: not meeting Bands 1–3; always non-material.
  Expert judgments for Bands 2–3 are documented; the assessment is reviewed annually in MA and ICLAAP updates.

- ESG Risk Appetite Framework (RAF) sets dedicated ESG risk statements, metrics, limits, and governance to ensure Nordea’s risk profile:
  - aligns with strategic sustainability objectives and financed emissions targets,
  - avoids disruptive business model shifts,
  - limits cross-risk ESG concentrations,
  - and stays within defined Level 2/3 limits for underlying prudential risks.

- An ESG Risk Appetite Statement (RAS), introduced in 2019 and since enhanced, mandates prudent management of material ESG risks across all prudential risks, customer engagement to align with the Paris Agreement, and progressive reduction in financed emissions.

- ESG RAF metrics (at Levels 1–3) are designed considering:
  - aggregation across the Group and links to long-term strategy,
  - relevance within the risk taxonomy and material ESG factor exposure,
  - strategic ambition, including financed emissions commitments and exclusions,
  - alignment among metrics (e.g., restatement tolerances vs. emissions trajectory).

- Metrics and limits are consistently defined and measured across units; governance for monitoring, reporting, and breach escalation is set by the Sustainability and ESG Policy Framework.

- Board-approved limits and KRIs for financed emissions (loans to the public) were introduced in 2021. In 2024, Group Level 1 financed emissions limits were tightened to meet GHG targets and cascaded as Level 2 limits to business areas, based on 2019 baselines and 2030 targets, requiring year-on-year declines.

- Lending and investment strategies set limits on exposures to harmful/controversial activities. Public sector guidelines (forestry, real estate, shipping, agriculture, gambling, fossil fuels, defense, mining) define exclusions, requirements, and customer engagement expectations for Paris alignment.

- Implementation across risk types: industry credit policies embed sector guideline requirements in lending and origination; Illiquid Exposures investments apply detailed ESG analysis and a separate ESG rating in due diligence aligned with minimum requirements and long-term targets.

- Further details on ESG strategy, risk management, and governance are provided in environmental, social, and governance sub-sections.

- Climate-related physical risks: Nordea defines specific risk drivers under its ESG Factor Taxonomy, with flooding identified as the most relevant risk to 2030, especially for real estate collateral (potential collateral devaluation). Mitigation relies on EPC data, corporate transition plans, customer ESG assessments, industry credit policies, monitoring of national adaptation and insurance availability, and environmental/building certifications and permits. Ongoing data development improves risk measurement, and dedicated risk appetite indicators for climate-related physical risks are included in the RAF.

- Nature-related risks: Nordea sets physical and transition risk drivers, with physical drivers including loss of tree cover and ecosystem condition/productivity, and transition drivers covering regulatory, technological, and societal changes. Some physical drivers (land, freshwater and sea use change, invasive species, water scarcity) are assessed as less relevant for Nordea’s business. Overall exposure is mainly transition-driven; credit exposure to highly vulnerable sectors is low, though aggregate exposures (e.g., real estate) can elevate total risk. Materiality is largely regulatory in nature.

- Quantification and analytics: Nordea applies an external biodiversity impact scoring (Finance for Biodiversity Foundation, 04/2023) to its lending portfolio, identifying highest biodiversity footprints in agriculture, animal husbandry, food processing & beverages, and materials. The bank is evaluating multiple biodiversity quantification approaches with commercial and academic partners, and in 2025 will continue quantifying biodiversity impacts and risks, refining data needs and understanding risk transmission to portfolios.

- Strategy, governance, and risk appetite: In 2023, Nordea published its first position on biodiversity and nature-related impacts and risks, including a Biodiversity Roadmap and commitments to embed biodiversity into strategy, governance, and risk management by 2025. Initial internal trainings have been conducted, and work has begun to extend nature-related targets in the Risk Appetite Framework. An initial 2023 risk appetite approach focuses on identifying, monitoring, and mitigating nature-related risks for large corporates in vulnerable industries.

- Existing commitments and sector policies: Nordea implements the Equator Principles for project finance and is a signatory to the Responsible Ship Recycling Standards and Poseidon Principles to address environmental and labor risks in shipping and to mitigate climate risks. In alignment with the UN Global Compact, commitments cover recycling, pollution prevention, and broader environmental safeguards. The current strategic ambition also targets mitigation of freshwater stress, resource scarcity, and water, air, and land contamination.

nodes.title: Capital & liquidity adequacy conclusion
nodes.heading: 2.1.3 Capital & liquidity adequacy conclusion
nodes.start_phrase: Capital adequacy assessment coverage for ESG -related impacts was initiated in 2020 and extended in 2021 to cover all prudential risk categories of Nordea’s Common Risk Taxonomy.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and approach: Nordea assesses ESG-related impacts on capital and liquidity across all prudential risk categories using a cross-risk view and a consistent 4-band materiality system within its ICLAAP/ICAAP framework.
- ICAAP conclusions: In 2024, capitalisation was evaluated per risk type and cross-risk. Additional capital was deemed necessary only for climate-related impacts on credit risk; no extra capital needed for other risks. Nordea maintains a strong capital position to cover this. All prudential risks except compliance and market risk are materially driven by ESG drivers; some ESG effects are already embedded in risk quantification.
- ILAAP conclusions: Environmental liquidity risks were quantified at Group level (2022, revisited 2023). In 2024, climate/nature-related hazards are most likely to affect HQLA and residential real estate–collateralised assets, with compounding chronic and acute water-related hazards most relevant. Liquidity ratios remain within limits except under very severe compounding scenarios; nature-related hazards are highly unlikely to affect liquidity. Overall liquidity buffers are sufficient for ESG-related risks.
- Stress testing program:
  - General: Annual ICLAAP includes climate-related stress tests and sensitivity analyses covering trading/banking books, liquidity, and strategic resilience.
  - Credit risk: Since 2020, short-term (3-year) transition scenarios via a GHG emissions tax show material impacts; methodologies enhanced using Scope 1–2 emissions and sector proxies. Physical risk tests since 2021 focus on Nordic drought/flooding. Long-term tests for net-zero alignment reveal high methodological uncertainty and dependence on customer/policy actions; climate-related credit risks are material in both short and long term.
  - Market risk: Short-term scenarios cover transition risk (NGFS Delayed Transition–based) and acute physical risk via an internal “Nordic flood risk on mortgage credit spreads” scenario aligned with credit/liquidity scenarios.
  - Liquidity risk (ILAAP): Short-term transition and flood scenarios indicate climate change is a material driver of asset liquidity, deposit, and off-balance-sheet risks, though impacts are assessed as low.
  - Operational risk: Transition risk drivers linked to legal and greenwashing effects are most material.
- Integration and development: From 2023, climate stress testing is embedded in ICAAP. In 2024, credit stress testing included a short-term transition scenario in a main ICAAP scenario, an expanded flood scenario, long-term portfolio projections under various transition paths, and a first-time sensitivity to biodiversity loss. Embedding aims to enhance learning and align stress testing with broader climate- and nature-related activities.

nodes.title: SOCIAL FACTORS
nodes.heading: 2.2 SOCIAL FACTORS
nodes.start_phrase: Nordea sees human rights as the foundation for the work within the Group’s social responsibility strategy and fundamental to ensuring a social license to operate and continued business growth.
nodes.summary:
The excerpt outlines Nordea’s social strategy and related risk management. It positions human rights as the foundation of Nordea’s social responsibility and business growth, implemented through the ESG Policy Framework for both own operations and financial counterparties, and aligned with UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights, the UN Global Compact, and the Equator Principles. It highlights priority SDGs—4 (Quality Education), 5 (Gender Equality), 8–10 (Decent Work and Inclusive Growth, Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure, Reduced Inequalities)—and emphasizes sector-sensitive human rights requirements. Internally, Nordea’s Code of Conduct covers stakeholder impacts, customer relationships, equality and diversity, human and labor rights, and financial crime control; annual Code training is mandatory, with optional human rights training, and policies address gender balance, non-discrimination, procurement, and sanctions (the latter indirectly managing social impacts). Stakeholder engagement is detailed in the Annual Report.

On risk management, Nordea’s ESG Factor Taxonomy defines social risk drivers and maps them to ESRS topics using a decision-tree approach based on its ICLAAP materiality process, linking ESRS S1–S4 to the Common Risk Taxonomy and assessing implications for credit, operational, and compliance risks. The materiality outcomes indicate S1 (own workforce—especially working conditions) and S4 (consumers and end users—customer relationships/information) are material from a financial risk perspective, while S2 (workers in the value chain) and S3 (affected communities) are assessed as non-material.

- 2024 DMA relevance assessment finds governance risk drivers can further impact these operational and compliance risks.

- Credit risk mitigation:
  - Governance factors embedded in ESG Factor Taxonomy and integrated into credit risk processes, mirroring environmental risk handling.
  - Industry and customer-level screening; governance issues incorporated into management risk scoring (governance model, planning, decisions, trustworthiness).
  - ESG rating override available when ESG impacts misalign with ratings.
  - Early Warning Indicators capture ESG events; ESG assessment required upon EWI trigger.
  - Due diligence includes KYC and Equator Principles for project finance.

  - Some governance risks partially covered through counterparty credit risk and management risk in ratings.

- Operational and compliance risks:
  - Relevant governance factors managed through the standard risk management framework.

- Risk control and monitoring:
  - Existing ESG Risk Appetite Framework includes governance risk metrics, reported periodically to the Board.
  - Metrics and limits cover financial reporting risks, including ESG-related misstatements and greenwashing in financial/regulatory disclosures.
  - Internal ICPs may include ESG-related exclusion criteria, including governance aspects.
  - Governance risk is embedded in the regular risk cycle; no additional capital allocation is deemed necessary.
